title: P1 — Port-range allocator leak: non-force destroy returns not_found after userdel failure WITHOUT freeing the range; TTL-expired agents exhausted the whole las-03 pool (proven 2026-09-03)
detail: PROVEN LIVE on bunker-las-03 (imhotep foreman tick T230, 2026-09-03 ~19:45Z): after the fleet-wide 17:11Z bunkerd restart, audit export shows 19 successful SpawnAgent vs 9 ok DestroyAgent + 15 not_found DestroyAgent → 19−9 = 10 = the ENTIRE pool (config port_range 30000-31000, 100/agent) held by agent IDs invisible to the registry. ListAgents = 0 agents while SpawnAgent failed 26x with 'port range allocation: no free port ranges available (pool exhausted: 10 ranges)' from 18:15Z to 19:48Z (QA spawn bursts 19:10-19:19Z + retries). Host also shows 48 bunker-* users persisting (many with RUNNING rootless dockerd processes) while the registry lists none. ROOT CAUSE CHAIN: internal/agent/manager_destroy.go Step 3 (~:63-73) — non-force destroy where userdel -rf fails (agent user still owns running processes: rootless dockerd/rootlesskit daemons) does m.tracker.Unregister(agentID) and returns Status not_found WITHOUT calling m.portAlloc.Free(agentID); Free only runs at ~:115 after full cleanup. The TTL reaper (manager.go reapExpiredAgents, 1-min ticker → Destroy non-force) is a frequent triggering caller: expired agent whose rootless dockerd didn't die in time → userdel fails → registry slot freed, port range leaked forever (allocator is in-memory; restart clears it, orphan users/daemons do NOT clear). Secondary defect: Step 1 dockerd stop (stopDockerdDirect + systemctl --user fallback) never WAITS for the rootlesskit/dockerd PIDs to actually exit before userdel -rf runs. FIX SKETCH: (1) call m.portAlloc.Free(agentID) in the not_found early-return path — unconditional, idempotent (Free no-ops for unknown IDs); (2) harden Step 1: after stop, poll up to ~10s for the agent user's rootlesskit/dockerd PIDs to exit, SIGKILL stragglers, then userdel; (3) same Free-before-return guarantee on any other early return between Allocate and the final Free. PASS: (1) unit test — non-force destroy with failing userdel returns not_found AND portAlloc.Available() is back to full; (2) unit test — force-mode destroy with failing userdel still frees; (3) TTL-reaper path covered — expired agent with a running process does not leak a range; (4) existing suite green; VERIFY-PASS evidence committed. OPS NOTE (not part of PASS): after fix deploys, las-03 needs a steward/Bane root pass to restart bunkerd (reclaims the 10 leaked ranges — sudo restart is approval-blocked in cron sessions) and to clean the 48 orphan bunker-* users + their dockerd daemons. Detection recipe for recurrence: bunker audit export → compare ok-spawn count vs ok-destroy count since last restart; delta > 0 = leaked ranges.

title: [P3] Port allocator is in-memory only — post-restart re-registration can double-allocate a live agent's range

title: P0 — [Bane 09-12, supersedes SPAWN-REG-001 + QA-BUNKER-4] Durable agent registry: bunkerd keeps its agent list ONLY in memory — every daemon restart (deploy/crash/reboot) loses all agent records while the Linux users, rootless dockerd stacks, and reserved port ranges persist. FIX (three parts): (1) PERSIST — append-only JSONL registry file (default /var/lib/bunkerd/agents.jsonl, 0600 root, rotation 5MB×3 matching the audit log pattern) recording spawn/heartbeat/destroy events; on daemon start, replay to rebuild the registry. SIZE CONTROL — the event log is size-capped (rotation above) AND a `bunker registry compact` admin command rewrites the log to the CURRENT RECONCILED STATE (one record per live agent — the compacted snapshot becomes the new source of truth; stale event history dropped). Compact is the documented maintenance path for long-lived hosts; it must lock against concurrent spawn/destroy writes (refuse or block briefly), be safe offline, and print before/after counts. (2) RECONCILE — on startup, compare registry vs system state (getent bunker-* users, /run/user/<uid>, port allocations): agents present in system but not registry = ORPHANS → policy flag reconciliation.mode: adopt|destroy (default destroy with a startup log line per action; adopt re-registers the agent). Registry entry but no system user = stale record → purge. (3) IDEMPOTENT DESTROY — destroy of an already-gone agent returns success (not_found is only for never-existed ids); non-force destroy must ALSO release the port range on userdel failure (QA-BUNKER-4 leak path). A user on any tagged release gets host-shared /tmp while reading docs that promise isolation. FIX (either side): cut a release containing 9703082 so tagged daemons match the README; AND make the daemon advertise capability/isolation level (ServerInfo field) with `bunker status`/`info` printing it, so silent downgrades become visible.

title: [P2] bunker mount fails reproducibly against a healthy agent with raw 'read: Connection reset by peer' — no retry, no actionable error
detail: On bunker-las-04 with agent df0916a (running, exec + docker + tunnel all healthy): `bunker mount df0916a /mnt` failed 2/2 times with `read: Connection reset by peer` + `bunker: sshfs failed: exit status 1`. Raw `ssh` to the agent works; the sftp subsystem answers (ssh -s sftp returns protocol banner); plain `sshfs` from the control host failed identically to the CLI, once in verbose mode showing auth success then 'remote host has disconnected' — consistent with sshd rate/parallel-session limiting (MaxStartups) on the many-connection agent host, where each sshfs attempt opens a fresh connection while existing tunnels/sessions are alive. FIX: add bounded retry with backoff to the mount command's sshfs invocation, and wrap the failure with 'sshfs connection reset — agent host may be limiting parallel SSH sessions; try again or close other tunnels'.

title: [P1] Every bunker-* SSH session on the demo host is DENIED (pam_open_session: System error) — exec/mount/cp are all broken against healthy, running agents; the provisioned GAP-075 PAM block demands a group membership the stale deployed daemon never grants
detail: LIVE (foreman tick 439, bunker-mvp, agent foreman-vrf-1789573645 — spawned and registered as RUNNING by the deployed daemon). SYMPTOM: ssh to the agent returns exit status 254 with the login banner as the only output and NO command output; sshfs reports 'remote host has disconnected' / 'read: Connection reset by peer'. sshd journal per connection: 'pam_unix(sshd:session): session opened for user bunker-<id>(uid=1010)' then 'error: PAM: pam_open_session(): System error'. The daemon's flagship workflow (exec over SSH, mount, cp) therefore cannot work on the demo host at all while the daemon reports the agent running. ROOT CAUSE, ONE COMMAND: /etc/pam.d/sshd carries the GAP-075 block — classifier `pam_succeed_if user !~ bunker-*`, then `[success=ignore default=die] pam_exec.so quiet /usr/lib/bunker/pam-tmp-guard verify bunker-agents`, then `required pam_namespace.so`. `PAM_USER=<fresh agent> /usr/lib/bunker/pam-tmp-guard verify bunker-agents` → 'bunker-pam-guard: user <id> is not a member of bunker-agents', rc=1 → pam_exec maps non-zero to PAM_SYSTEM_ERR → `default=die` denies the session. An OLDER agent that is in the group passes (PAM_USER=bunker-imgspec-none → rc=0) and its SSH works, so the discriminator is GROUP MEMBERSHIP, not agent health. Host has the SSH-side provision (drop-in + helper dated 2026-09-13) while /opt/bunker/bunkerd is the 2026-08-30 build that predates the spawn-side 'isolation-provision' stage that adds new agents to bunker-agents — host provisioned, daemon too old = every agent that daemon spawns is locked out of SSH. FIX: (1) restore congruence — deploy the HEAD daemon to the demo so spawn grants the membership (this is the DF-BUNKER-10 lag class and it must happen before ANY live exec/mount verification on the demo can be trusted); or `bunker host-provision --uninstall --apply` to return to shared /tmp — never hand-delete only the drop-in, whose own comment warns that the remaining pam_exec precondition then fails closed and locks EVERY bunker-* session out; (2) make the skew impossible — host-provision refuses (or loudly warns) when the installed daemon is older than the hardening it installs, and spawn grants the membership BEFORE the agent is reported ready; (3) operator-facing — `bunker exec` surfaces the session-denial cause instead of a bare exit 254. PASS: (1) a freshly spawned agent on the demo host accepts `bunker exec <id> -- whoami` with real output (no 254) and `bunker mount <id>` succeeds; (2) a test proves the provision/daemon version-skew check rejects an older daemon; (3) spawn reports ready only after an SSH exec probe succeeds. RELATED / REFUTES: DF-BUNKER-14 (mount fails against a healthy agent) blames the CLI's fixed `-o allow_other`; that is REFUTED live — sshfs with allow_other AND without it fail identically against the same agent, the raw SFTP channel is clean (.hushlogin changes nothing), and a plain `ssh` to that agent already fails with 254.

reasoning.note: Found while verifying DF-BUNKER-14's premise live. The chain a later tick must not re-derive: the sshd PAM journal line, the one-command guard reproduction, and the membership discriminator between a locked-out fresh agent and a working older one. Filed separately from DF-BUNKER-14 so the mount row closes against the right root cause instead of an allow_other fallback that fixes nothing.

title: [P1] First post-INT-CI-008 tree is red at JOB level on BOTH jobs (run 35142150138, sha 7321f2c, 19:42Z): every spawn dies at stage rootless-install with 'Failed to start docker.service: Unit docker.service not found' — 7 root-suite TestSpawn_* tests fail and the E2E battery fails 2 cells, because the agent's systemd user manager cannot start the docker.service unit the rootless installer just wrote
detail: ATTRIBUTION (foreman tick 443, job-level only — run 35142150138 reports conclusion=success at run level because root-suite and regression both carry continue-on-error). Run 35142150138 (sha 7321f2c) is the first completed run whose tree CONTAINS the INT-CI-008 fix bb751f5, and it is red at job level twice: (a) root-suite job step 'Root-gated suite (TestSpawn|TestCgroup|TestConcurrency)' FAILURE — TestSpawn_WithProvidedAgentID, _GeneratesSSHKeys, _PersistsSSHKey, _DiskMaxBytesEnforced, _TmpDirExists, _AuthorizedKeysHasEnvironment, _SystemdUnitHasUlimits all fail; (b) regression job step 'E2E battery' FAILURE — PASS 31 / FAIL 2 with the battery's own spawn red ('✗ spawn agent — Creating agent...'), CERTIFIED BINARY MATCH (commit reported 7321f2c). SHARED SIGNATURE in both jobs: 'spawn <id> failed at stage rootless-install: install rootless docker for bunker-<id>: run rootless installer as bunker-<id>: exit status 1' and, from the rootless installer itself, 'Failed to start docker.service: Unit docker.service not found.' (17 occurrences in the run log), preceded in the daemon log by 'agent user manager unreachable; transient unit disable skipped ... reason=no user session bus ... Failed to connect to bus: No medium found'. MECHANISM (as far as the evidence goes, do not overclaim): the rootless installer writes ~/.config/systemd/user/docker.service and immediately runs `systemctl --user start docker.service`; when the agent's user manager is not up/reachable at that moment the unit is unknown to it. This is the same FAMILY as INT-CI-007/INT-CI-008 (user-manager bring-up on a contended shared host) but a DIFFERENT stage (rootless-install, not user-manager-start) and it is NOT the INT-CI-008 symptom (that one carried 'user-manager-start failed: unit user@<uid>.service is-active=failed' with the pam_systemd runtime-dir stat error and is fixed at bb751f5). CONCURRENCY: the root-suite job's spawns ran 19:52-19:54Z while the regression job's battery spawns ran 19:44-19:52Z, i.e. the two jobs spawn agents on the SAME self-hosted host in overlapping windows — the contention question must be answered by evidence, not assumed. FIX DIRECTION: (1) make the rootless-install stage prove the agent's user manager is reachable (and start it / reset-failed + retry once) BEFORE running the installer, and make the installer's `systemctl --user start` retry after a daemon-reload, so a freshly written unit is never 'not found'; (2) if the evidence shows the two jobs contend, serialize the CI jobs that spawn agents on the shared host (or give the battery and the root-suite disjoint spawn budget) instead of running them concurrently. PASS: (1) a run on a tree carrying the fix is 4/4 job-level green with the spawn steps passing, verified by expanding .jobs[] (run-level success is NOT acceptable evidence); (2) a test proves the rootless-install stage fails with an actionable cause naming the user-manager state when the manager is unreachable, and succeeds after the manager is brought up; (3) 'Unit docker.service not found' no longer appears in a run log; (4) if contention is the mechanism, the CI workflow serializes the spawning jobs and the row records the before/after window overlap.

title: [P1] Spawn reports an agent ready without proving its SSH session works - implement the bounded SSH exec probe (the remaining conjunct of INT-DEMO-001 criterion 3)

title: [P1] spawn fails at rootless-install when the allocated uid is recycled (previous owner's user@<uid> manager still active -> session-bus daemon-reload fails) and the failed-spawn rollback leaks the linger entry
detail: [P1] spawn dies at stage rootless-install whenever the freshly allocated uid was RECYCLED from an agent whose systemd user manager is still live, and the failed-spawn rollback leaks the linger entry. MEASURED (foreman tick 450, bunker-mvp, HEAD 1872d22, deployed daemon 0.1.4/1872d22): the standalone E2E gate's nested regression suite ran 14 red cells, ALL cascade from one spawn. The daemon's own attribution (/var/log/bunkerd-regression.log): 'spawn entering stage regr-alpha stage=rootless-install' -> WARN 'agent user manager unreachable from the agent session before the rootless install' user=bunker-regr-alpha unit=user@1002.service state='unit user@1002.service: is-active=active (Result=success)' linger_entries=3 -> WARN 'userdel failed; terminating user processes and retrying' error='userdel bunker-regr-alpha: exit status 8 (output: userdel: user bunker-regr-alpha is currently used by process 2168325)' -> ERROR 'spawn failed stage=rootless-install error=... daemon-reload through the session bus failed; unit user@1002.service: is-active=active (Result=success); linger entries: 3'. uid 1002 had been used minutes earlier by a destroyed agent in the same gate run (foreman-idemo-*), and systemctl showed user@1002.service still ACTIVE at spawn time (it only went 'failed (Result: signal)' when the rollback killed it). SECOND DEFECT IN THE SAME PATH: the rollback of a failed spawn does NOT un-linger - after the run /var/lib/systemd/linger held bunker-regr-alpha, bunker-1dd412d0 and bunker-ff86d69a while none of those users existed (the destroy path DOES un-linger, proven tick 441; the failed-spawn rollback path apparently does not). All three were pruned with the deployed `bunker linger prune` (scanned 4, stale removed 3, kept 1 live). WHY IT WAS INVISIBLE: the pre-INT-CI-012 harness printed 'regression suite PASSED' over the nested suite's 'PASS: 16 / FAIL: 14' (see INT-CI-012). FIX DIRECTION: (1) in the rootless-install stage, treat an ACTIVE user manager for the allocated uid as a live signal, not a failure: the reachability probe's `systemctl --user daemon-reload` must not fail the spawn when user@<uid>.service is active for a DIFFERENT (recycled) user name - either assert the runtime dir/bus belongs to the agent's own user before probing, or retry after resetting the stale manager for that uid; (2) never allocate a uid whose user manager is still active (or stop/terminate it as part of spawn's fresh-uid preparation); (3) make the failed-spawn rollback un-linger exactly like destroy does. PASS: (a) a test proves spawn succeeds (or fails with an attribution naming the recycled uid) when the allocated uid's previous user manager is still active; (b) a live repro on the demo host: spawn an agent, destroy it, immediately spawn again (uid recycled) -> spawn completes; (c) `ls /var/lib/systemd/linger` is unchanged across a FAILED spawn (rollback un-lingers); (d) the nested regression suite's 14 spawn/exec/list cells go green in the standalone gate.
reasoning: Surfaced by the live standalone gate AFTER INT-CI-012's harness fix restored an honest nested verdict: the 14 red cells were previously reported as 'regression suite PASSED'. The attribution comes from the daemon's own breadcrumb (stage + unit state + userdel conflict + linger count), not from a guess, and the uid was demonstrably recycled inside one gate run.

title: [P1] spawn dies at rootless-install with 'Failed to connect to bus: No medium found' because the readiness gate is a socket-file stat, not a bus handshake: the manager is up (is-active=active, dbus.socket Listening) while the agent session cannot connect
detail: [P1] MEASURED tick 453 on bunker-mvp with the INT-SPAWN-002 fix deployed (87aa282 applied to /opt/bunker, rebuilt, installed, bunkerd restarted): the standalone nested suite still reports PASS=16 / FAIL=14 and EVERY red cell is a spawn that dies at stage rootless-install. The new attribution (INT-SPAWN-002 C1) names the real error for the first time, verbatim: session_probe='Failed to connect to bus: No medium found' with unit user@1002.service is-active=active (Result=success) and linger_entries=8. Journal for the same second (16:10:25-16:10:27Z) shows the manager coming up cleanly - 'Starting user@1002.service', 'Listening on dbus.socket', 'systemctl --user set-environment DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS=unix:path=/run/user/1002/bus' - then the su session (pam_unix(su-l:session) opened and closed) fails with ENOMEDIUM 0.7s later, the recovery stops the unit, a NEW manager starts, and the SECOND probe fails with the same error. The one-shot recovery therefore runs to completion and the failure reproduces immediately after it. NOT THE MECHANISM (disproved by controlled probes on the production daemon the same tick): (a) same-name uid recycling alone - spawn/destroy/spawn of tick453-alpha reused uid 1002 and succeeded twice with exec OK; (b) an ACTIVE manager for a deleted account - spawn tick453-beta, userdel -rf only (user@1003 is-active=active, logind record gone), spawn tick453-gamma on the recycled uid 1003 succeeded with exec OK. The stale-logind-record WARN of INT-SPAWN-002 did NOT fire during the failing run. LEADING HYPOTHESIS (not yet proven): waitForUserManager only polls os.Stat(<runtimeDir>/bus) - it returns as soon as the socket PATH exists, which is not evidence that the bus accepts a connection; in the failing runs the probe arrives ~0.7s after a fresh manager start and libdbus answers ENOMEDIUM. FIX DIRECTION: replace the stat with a bounded BUS-LEVEL readiness check (repeat the real session-side probe - or an equivalent connect/handshake - inside the existing userManagerWaitTimeout budget, treating 'socket exists but will not answer' as NOT READY rather than as the final attribution), then attribute honestly when the budget is exhausted. Keep the one-shot recovery semantics and the zero-destructive-action healthy path. PASS: (1) the nested suite's spawn cells go green on the demo host (tally PASS=30 / FAIL=0 or, at minimum, the rootless-install failures gone) OR a first-attempt probe that is refused-while-the-manager-is-starting is explicitly retried within the budget and the spawn then succeeds; (2) a unit test proves the readiness loop retries a not-yet-answering socket and still fails bounded and attributed when the manager never answers; (3) the healthy path still probes once with zero destructive calls. EVIDENCE: /var/log/bunkerd-regression.log on bunker-mvp (16:10:25-16:10:28Z), journalctl -u user@1002.service for the same window.

title: [P1] `su -` RESETS the session environment, so userSessionEnv's XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS never reach the agent session: the probe gets NEITHER variable and systemctl answers 'Failed to connect to bus: No medium found' - a PERMANENT condition in any daemon not launched by systemd (the standalone gate's nested suite), not the readiness race INT-SPAWN-003 assumed
detail: [P1] MEASURED tick 454 on bunker-mvp (78.46.173.180) with the INT-SPAWN-003 fix deployed (a499216 installed to /usr/local/bin/bunker+bunkerd, nested regression suite run standalone on its own ports, log /tmp/tick454-nested.log, daemon log /var/log/bunkerd-regression.log). The nested suite is STILL PASS=16 / FAIL=14 and every red cell is a spawn dying at stage rootless-install. The new readiness wait proves the condition is PERMANENT rather than a late-answering bus: 16:38:09.324Z INFO retry line (first probe refused, session_probe='Failed to connect to bus: No medium found', unit user@1002.service is-active=active), 16:38:39.387Z the FULL-30s-budget exhaustion WARN + one-shot recycled-uid recovery, 16:38:40.167Z the recovery's own readiness wait starts and burns ANOTHER 30s (16:39:10.204Z final attribution, same error). ~60s of probing across a manager teardown+bring-up without a single successful answer. ROOT CAUSE, PROVEN BY CONTROLLED PROBES THIS TICK (all commands run as root on the host): (1) `su -` RESETS THE ENVIRONMENT - `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=/run/user/1002 DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS=unix:path=/run/user/1002/bus su - kara -c 'echo XDG=[$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR] DBUS=[$DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS]'` prints `XDG=[] DBUS=[]`, so the env userSessionEnv sets on the `su` process (internal/agent/rootless.go userSessionEnv, called by runUserSessionCmd/runRootlessInstallerCmd) is STRIPPED before the probe runs - the file comment claiming the values are 'layered on top of the inherited environment' and 'the installer call uses the SAME construction' is factually wrong for `su -`; (2) the EXACT error text is the no-variable case - `env -u DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS -u XDG_RUNTIME_DIR systemctl --user daemon-reload` on the same host prints verbatim 'Failed to connect to bus: No medium found'; (3) IN-BAND injection works - `su - kara -c "XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=/run/user/1002 DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS=unix:path=/run/user/1002/bus sh -c 'echo \$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR'"` prints `/run/user/1002`; (4) the CONTRAST that makes this host-context-dependent: the systemd-launched production daemon on this same host (env carries NEITHER variable) spawns agents successfully, and the host journal records NO pam_systemd 'New session ... of user bunker-<id>' line for the failing su calls (only pam_unix su-l session open/close), so no login stack provides the bus address in that context either - the mechanism behind the contrast (why pam_systemd registers no session for the su child in the non-systemd case) is the ONE thing still unmeasured. FIX DIRECTION: stop relying on the su process environment - build the session environment INSIDE the command the session runs (e.g. `su - <user> -c 'XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=<dir> DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS=unix:path=<dir>/bus systemctl --user daemon-reload'`, or a `env ... sh -c` wrapper) for the probe, the daemon-reload retry AND the rootless installer call, keeping one shared construction so INT-CI-009's 'same env for every user-session command' property becomes TRUE instead of aspirational; add a live-faithful unit test that fails against a runner which sets cmd.Env only. PASS: (1) the nested suite's spawn cells go green on the demo host (the 14 red cells clear; tally PASS=30 / FAIL=0) OR a controlled repro shows the probe succeeding in the non-systemd daemon context; (2) a unit test proves the session command carries the bus address in-band and the probe no longer depends on pam_systemd setting anything; (3) the healthy production path is unchanged (probe succeeds, zero destructive calls, one probe when the bus answers immediately); (4) go build/vet/test/gofmt clean. EVIDENCE: /var/log/bunkerd-regression.log 16:38:08-16:39:13Z on bunker-mvp, the four controlled probes above, /tmp/tick454-nested.log. MECHANISM MEASURED (same tick, two probes on the host, 16:48Z): running the SAME su from a logind session vs from a non-session context flips pam_systemd's behaviour. (A) from the ssh login session that launches the standalone gate: `su - kara -c 'echo XDG=[$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR] DBUS=[$DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS]'` -> `XDG=[] DBUS=[]` (no bus address); (B) the production-daemon shape, a transient service outside any logind session: `systemd-run --quiet --wait --pipe --unit=tick454-probe su - kara -c ...` -> `XDG=[/run/user/1001] DBUS=[unix:path=/run/user/1001/bus]`. pam_systemd therefore sets the bus environment for the su session ONLY when the calling process is not already inside a logind session; when the daemon descends from an ssh login session it provides nothing, and because `su -` strips the caller's environment the agent session ends up with NEITHER variable. That is why the production systemd daemon and the CI runner (both services, no logind session) spawn fine while the ssh-launched standalone gate fails 100% - the same binary, the same host, a different launch context. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE FIX: the session bus environment must be built IN-BAND (inside the command the session runs) and must never depend on pam_systemd or on the su process environment; probe (3) above already proves the in-band form reaches the child.

title: [P1] build-and-test / Unit tests is RED on a board-only commit (run 35253802213, sha 58546f5): TestServerInfo fails its own UptimeSeconds guard (service_test.go:702) with a mechanism the guard cannot explain, and the same internal/server run makes a REAL public-CA call to acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org for bunker.example.com (rejectedIdentifier) - the other three CI jobs skip on `needs`, so each such flake costs a whole push its coverage
detail: [P1] The Tier-0 CI job `build-and-test` FAILED at step 'Unit tests' on a BOARD-ONLY commit, so the other three jobs (regression, root-suite, gitreins-guard) were SKIPPED by `needs` and the push got zero coverage. EVIDENCE (GitHub run 35253802213, repo deployBunker/bunker, headSha 58546f5, created 2026-09-17T17:36:49Z - board JSONL + .gitreins/tasks.yaml only, no .go change): `gh run view ... --json jobs` = build-and-test failure (failed step 'Unit tests'), regression/root-suite/gitreins-guard skipped. FAILED ASSERTION, verbatim: `--- FAIL: TestServerInfo (0.00s)` / `service_test.go:702: ServerInfo().UptimeSeconds is 0, want seconds since daemon start` / `FAIL github.com/deployBunker/bunker/internal/server 1.019s` - the ONLY red in the run. WHY THE GUARD DOES NOT EXPLAIN IT: the assertion is `if msg.UptimeSeconds == 0 && time.Since(serverStartTime) >= time.Second` (internal/server/service_test.go:701) and both sides read the same package var `serverStartTime = time.Now()` (internal/server/service.go:37) via `uint64(time.Since(serverStartTime).Seconds())` (service.go:97). With elapsed >= 1s the value cannot be 0, and with elapsed < 1s the test must NOT fail - so this is NOT a simple razor-edge flake as the comment above it asserts ('CI: UHLP-145 razor-edge pattern; bunker FLAKE-001'). The mechanism is UNKNOWN as of filing and must be reproduced before it is fixed; the observable fact is that the same tree's Go tests passed in run 35251913868 (sha 95e55a8, 18 minutes earlier, build-and-test success) and in the foreman's local `go test ./... -count=1` on this tick (internal/server ok 1.293s). SECOND, INDEPENDENT DEFECT VISIBLE IN THE SAME LOG: during the internal/server package run the test binary made a REAL public-CA call - `info done waiting on internal rate limiter {"identifiers": ["bunker.example.com"], "ca": "https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory"}`, `info using ACME account .../acct/3760420716`, then `error obtain could not get certificate from issuer ... urn:ietf:params:acme:error:rejectedIdentifier - Cannot issue for bunker.example.com: forbidden by policy`. certmagic's async obtain for bunker.example.com escapes the test-side CA override (TestBuildTLSConfig_AutoTLSProducesConfig points certmagic.DefaultACME.CA at https://127.0.0.1:14000/dir and restores it in t.Cleanup, so a background obtain that starts after cleanup uses the REAL production CA). A unit test must never contact a public CA: it is nondeterministic, it depends on runner network egress, and here it produced a 400 from Let's Encrypt's policy check. FIX DIRECTION: (1) reproduce the uptime failure deterministically (run the package with `-count=20` and `-race` on CI-like hardware; print serverStartTime and time.Since(serverStartTime) inside the failing assertion to settle whether the var is being mutated or the elapsed measurement is the liar) and then fix the assertion so it can only fail for a real cause; (2) isolate certmagic in unit tests - for EVERY test that builds an auto_tls config, point certmagic.DefaultACME.CA at a local ACME test server for the WHOLE test lifetime (or set a certmagic config that never starts an async obtain) and assert the test made zero calls to acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org; (3) consider making the Tier-0 job's job-level conclusion the CI gate rather than the run-level one, so a single flaky unit test does not silently skip the regression + root-suite coverage. CORROBORATION ADDED WITHIN THE SAME TICK (evidence of NON-DETERMINISM, not a one-off): the very next board-only push from this tick (sha 0505b15, run 35255115947) ran the SAME Tier-0 job on the SAME ubuntu-latest runner and build-and-test came back COMPLETED/SUCCESS, while run 35253802213 (sha 58546f5) failed at 'Unit tests' ten minutes earlier - so this is a flake with a real but rare trigger, and the first fix step is a reproduction loop (`go test ./internal/server/ -count=50 -race`, instrumented with the two values), NOT a code change based on the current hypothesis. detail: INT-CI-014 sized the Tier 2 compaction valve from measurement (0.005 x 16M = 80,000 tokens per segment, so a 200-iteration run fires 2 compactions). Do NOT revert to 0.90 - that provably never fires.

title: [P1] A spawn that lands on a UID still carrying the previous agent's systemd state hangs 5 minutes, fails `user manager did not start`, and the rollback fails too — leaving an orphan user+home+linger entry that no API surface reports
detail:
MEASURED LIVE 2026-09-18 on bunker-las-02 (v0.1.4 = HEAD 967c331), reproduced through the daemon's own log trail.
CLIENT VIEW: POST SpawnAgent {"agent_id":"df0918-ttl","ttl":"2m"} -> no response at all for 300s (the client's documented request_timeout) -> socket TimeoutError. With a 330s client timeout the real answer arrives at 5m0.001s: HTTP 500, 154B, {"code":"internal"}. There is no progress signal, no streaming, no way to tell 'slow spawn' from 'dead spawn'.
DAEMON LOG (journalctl -u bunkerd): creating user -> persisted SSH private key -> starting rootless dockerd -> 'resetting user manager runtime' uid=1012 runtime_dir=/run/user/1012 -> 'lazily unmounted stale runtime mount' -> 5 MINUTES OF SILENCE -> 'rolling back: removing user' -> ERROR 'rollback userdel failed' error="context deadline exceeded" -> ERROR 'spawn agent failed' error="install rootless docker for bunker-df0918-ttl: user manager did not start for bunker-df0918-ttl: context deadline exceeded" -> '500 154B in 5m0.001132966s'.
RESIDUE LEFT (the data-loss/blast-radius part): the rollback reuses the already-expired spawn context, so `userdel` fails and the host keeps /etc/passwd uid 1012 bunker-df0918-ttl, /home/bunker-df0918-ttl (36K, partially installed) and a FRESH linger entry /var/lib/systemd/linger/bunker-df0918-ttl. The key /etc/bunkerd/ssh/df0918-ttl WAS removed by the rollback. GetAgent df0918-ttl -> 404 not_found: the daemon has no record of any of it, and neither `bunker list` nor `bunker status` can show or clean it.
HOST STATE THAT CORRELATES: UID 1012 previously belonged to a deleted agent (bunker-59bd09c1) whose user-1012.slice was STILL ACTIVE since 2026-09-14 (3 days; `systemctl is-active user-1012.slice` = active) with no matching /etc/passwd user, 145 lingering bunker-* entries in /var/lib/systemd/linger, stale /run/user/1002..1008 dirs, 5 orphan homes and 4 orphan keys. CONTROL EXPERIMENT: after deleting the residue user+home at the operator level, a new spawn that landed on the SAME UID 1012 succeeded normally in 21.8s ('dockerd ready' -> 'agent registered' -> 'spawned successfully', then destroyed cleanly) — so the host is healthy once the stale per-UID state is gone. Hypothesis for the worker to prove (NOT claimed as established): useradd reuses a freed UID while the old occupant's user-<uid>.slice / linger entry / /run/user/<uid> persist, so the new agent's systemd --user manager cannot start inside the spawn deadline. title: [P1] docs/integration.md documents ExecAgent as server-streaming but gives no REST recipe — the §2-documented call returns a bare 415 with NO {"code","message"} envelope
detail:
MEASURED LIVE 2026-09-18 against bunker-las-02 (v0.1.4 = HEAD 967c331) with a stdlib REST client written from docs/integration.md alone (no CLI, no protobuf).
(a) The documented call fails opaquely: POST /bunker.v1.Bunkerd/ExecAgent with Content-Type: application/json (exactly what §2 prescribes) -> HTTP 415 Unsupported Media Type, Content-Length: 0, EMPTY body. §2 promises 'Errors carry a JSON {"code","message"} envelope and a real HTTP status', so a doc-following integrator gets neither a hint nor a code. 30+ minutes of the run went into reverse-engineering the surface.
(b) The working shape is connect streaming and is documented NOWHERE: Content-Type: application/connect+json; request body = [flags:1][len:4 BE][json] envelopes; response 200 + Transfer-Encoding: chunked; stdout/stderr arrive as protojson base64 bytes one envelope per write; exitCode only present when non-zero; final frame is a flags=0x02 trailer. `Connect-Protocol-Version: 1` is NOT required (verified).
(c) Both spec-shaped end-of-stream endings are rejected, and both are delivered as HTTP 200 with the error INSIDE the stream: trailing single byte 0x02 -> {"error":{"code":"invalid_argument","message":"protocol error: incomplete envelope: unexpected EOF"}}; trailing [0x02][0x00000000] envelope -> {"error":{"code":"internal","message":"unmarshal end stream message: unexpected end of JSON input"}}. A client that checks only the status code reads these as success with empty output. Only 'no EOS envelope, let Content-Length end the request' works.
Residual of DF-BUNKER-19 (which documented the unary response shapes): the streaming half was never covered.
FIX: add a copy-pasteable streaming example (curl/python) to docs/integration.md §5 + a §2 sentence naming the connect content-type as the streaming exception, AND return a real {"code","message"} envelope for the 415 (or a MediaType error) so the failure is self-explaining. PASS: (1) the doc contains a runnable ExecAgent-over-REST example that returns command output; (2) the wrong content-type produces a JSON envelope naming the expected type; (3) a test asserts the envelope. Evidence: docs/dogfood/2026-09-18-integration.md §4.1-4.3.

title: [P1] ExecAgent corrupts the HTTP response when a command writes to BOTH stdout and stderr - two goroutines call connect's unlocked ServerStream.Send concurrently (0/10 decodable responses on bunker-las-02; the daemon logs 'superfluous response.WriteHeader' at the same second)
detail:
SURFACED BY DF-BUNKER-22's live verification and NOT fixed there (that row touches no exec behavior; this one does).
MEASURED 2026-09-18 against bunker-las-02 (v0.1.4, commit cef10fc) with the stdlib REST client committed in DF-BUNKER-22, exec-only against the pre-existing agent kara-lair (no spawns/destroys): stdout-only 'echo OUT' = 10/10 framing intact; stderr-only 'echo ERR 1>&2' = 10/10; silent 'true' = 5/5; BOTH pipes ('echo OUT; echo ERR 1>&2') = 0/10 decodable. INDEPENDENT FOREMAN REPRO = 3/3 failed, three different failure texts ('truncated envelope: flags=0x31 needs 1628244480 bytes, 102 left'; and twice a body whose raw bytes carry the envelope frames followed by the literal 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK' status line).
RAW WIRE (raw socket on the las-02 loopback, ~half the attempts): the status line/header block, a chunk framer and the same envelope bytes appear interleaved and duplicated in one response, e.g. body bytes preceding the status line entirely: '\x00\x00\x00\x00\x15{"stderr":"RVJSCg=="}\x00\x00\x00\x00\x15{"stdout":"T1VUCg=="}HTTP/1.1 200 OK'.
TWO WRITERS ARE PRODUCING ONE RESPONSE.
DAEMON JOURNAL at the same second: 'http: superfluous response.WriteHeader call from github.com/go-chi/chi/v5/middleware.(*basicWriter).Write (wrap_writer.go:99)' and the WriteHeader variant (wrap_writer.go:91), 2 lines, bunker-las-02 bunkerd[269333].
CAUSE (strongly indicated, not proven end to end): internal/server/service.go ExecAgent starts ONE goroutine per pipe and each calls connect's ServerStream.Send directly; connect@v1.20.0 protocol_connect.go:809 Send() is unlocked and both goroutines flush through the same http.ResponseWriter. Clients cannot work around it (the corruption is in the byte stream, not in framing the client controls). Documented workaround in docs/integration.md: merge the streams inside the agent ('... 2>&1').
FIX: serialize the stream writes (a mutex around Send, or a single writer goroutine fed by both pipes) so concurrent pipe readers cannot interleave into one response.
PASS: (1) test pins it - a command writing to BOTH pipes produces a decodable stream with both payloads intact over repeated runs; (2) LIVE on bunker-mvp after deploy: a both-pipe command decodes 10/10 with stdout AND stderr present and the exit code faithful, while stdout-only/stderr-only stay 10/10; (3) no behavior change for single-stream commands; (4) AGENTS.md applies (exec-path change): live E2E battery VERIFY-PASS evidence committed.
Evidence: docs/dogfood/2026-09-18-integration-rest-streaming.md 4.1-4.4 (rates, wire bytes, journal, code pointer).

detail: Found while fixing GAP-079 (the docker-sock tunnel orphan); the SAME shape - a long-lived child spawned under a context that the CLI cancels with `defer cancel()` and no signal handling, so an abrupt CLI death runs nothing and the child is reparented to init: (1) internal/cli/cp.go:107 and internal/cli/deploy.go:94 build `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(..., 30s)` with `defer cancel()` and then run `exec.CommandContext(ctx, "scp"/"ssh", ...)` (cp.go:155, cp.go:173, deploy.go:142, deploy.go:162) - no Setpgid, no signal.NotifyContext. A SIGTERM to the CLI during a large transfer leaves scp running with no CLI attached, still writing to the remote host. (2) internal/cli/mount.go:255 runs each sshfs ATTEMPT under a 30s attempt context with the same pattern, so Ctrl-C during the mount window orphans the attempt (the established mount is a daemonised sshfs by design and is not part of this). (3) internal/cli/ssh.go:121 deliberately has no deadline (interactive; the terminal's foreground process group delivers Ctrl-C to the child) but a manager-issued SIGTERM to the CLI alone would still orphan the session - no Setpgid/reap. title: S6 HERMES SHIM: the translated tool surface, CONSTANT in size regardless of how many bunkers exist. title: S8 PER-SESSION TOOL ENABLE/DISABLE + EXECUTION-STATE ISOLATION: a Hermes session must be able to enable and disable its own tools dynamically, and a tool loaded for one session must never reuse another session's state. Measured gap today: `hermes chat -t <toolsets>` is genuinely per-run but ephemeral and start-time-only, while the persistent surface `hermes tools enable|disable` writes ONE global config - agent.disabled_toolsets and plugins.disabled in a single config.yaml read by every session on the box. So enabling a tool for one session currently toggles a global: the same shared-mutable-pointer shape as the active_server routing bug. Design rule (Rule B of the PRD): a session's ENABLED SET is session state, never global config - enabling a verb for this session writes one row (this session's own) and re-projects the tool list for this session only. Pair it with the sharing rule: registration metadata (name, JSON schema, description) is SHARED and immutable, while EXECUTION state (MCP client connection, plugin instance, LSP session, caches, lease handles, open file handles) is PER SESSION and never pooled - a pooled stateful client handed from session A to B would leak subscriptions, working directory, half-open files, cached reads and LSP document state. Mechanically the session tool list is: constant catalog -> this session's enabled row -> per-session projection into the system prompt -> dispatch against THIS session's enabled set (an unenabled verb refuses as tool_not_enabled_in_session, distinct from capability_unavailable) -> any instance created is keyed (session_id, tool) and released at session end. NO per-session re-registration is required, and no per-bunker registration either. PASS: (1) SESSION ISOLATION: two concurrent sessions; A disables a tool while B keeps it, then both toggle a different tool in the same minute - each session's offered list matches only its own choices, B is unaffected both ways, and the global config's disabled_toolsets / plugins.disabled are byte-identical before and after; (2) NO-STATE-REUSE: A loads a stateful tool and leaves it warm (cached read / open path / LSP document), then B loads the same tool and gets a fresh instance with no A-derived state - proved by asserting B's instance does not contain A's distinguishable artifact; (3) DYNAMIC: a mid-session enable/disable takes effect for that session on its next turn without a restart and without touching another session; (4) NO-STRANDING: killing a session holding per-session state reclaims its instances instead of stranding them, and a later session's footprint is unaffected; (5) the refusal for an unenabled verb is distinct from the refusal for an unsupported one; (6) a documented memory budget: per-session state scales with CONCURRENTLY ACTIVE sessions, not total starts.
detail: PRD S8, Rule B. The user's requirement is that tool enable/disable be session-local and that loaded tool state never be reused across sessions; today the persistent surface is global config, so a session toggling a tool changes what every other session is offered. This is the tools-side twin of the routing bug GAP-093 fixes.

title: MOUNT LIFECYCLE: proper cleanup, preflight, and a mountpoint a non-root user can actually use. MEASURED DEFECTS TODAY (verified 2026-09-20): (a) DEFAULT MOUNTPOINT IS UNUSABLE for a normal operator - mount.go:216 does os.MkdirAll(mountPoint, 0755) with a default of /mnt/bunker/<agent-id>, but /mnt here is root:root 0755 and /mnt/bunker does not exist, so the default path fails for any non-root user (the residual already noted under DF-BUNKER-14); (b) NO UNMOUNT PATH AT ALL - the command ends by PRINTING 'Unmount with: fusermount -u <path>' (mount.go:311) and there is no `bunker umount`, so cleanup is a manual shell incantation the operator must remember; (c) NO PREFLIGHT - the mount attempts without first establishing that the remote path EXISTS and is a DIRECTORY, so a dead/re-created agent (empty home) or a typo'd --path yields a mounted EMPTY tree that looks successful, which is precisely the 'writing to a non-existent thing' failure: an editor pointed at a successful-looking but empty mount writes into a fresh empty tree; (d) NO STALE-HANDLING - an interrupted mountpoint (dead FUSE session after a crashed sshfs or a killed network) is not detected, so the next attempt hits 'mountpoint is not empty' and the operator must clear it by hand. DELIVERABLE: (1) mountpoint policy - default under a USER-WRITABLE per-session root (e.g. $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/bunker/<agent-id> or ~/.bunker/mnt/<agent-id>), never a root-owned /mnt path, with the override honoured; (2) `bunker umount <agent-id|mountpoint>` that is idempotent (already-unmounted = success), clears a dead mountpoint via lazy unmount when needed, and reports what it did; (3) mount-time PREFLIGHT that verifies the remote path exists and is a directory BEFORE mounting and REFUSES with a named cause otherwise, so an empty tree can never be silently mounted; (4) stale/dirty mountpoint detection with an explicit recover path, and a clear refusal naming the holder when the mountpoint is live and in use; (5) a `bunker mount --json`/status surface listing live mounts (agent, mountpoint, remote path, pid) so cleanup is observable rather than remembered; (6) teardown on daemon/destroy of the agent - destroying an agent must not leave a dangling local mountpoint. PASS: (1) a non-root operator mounts with the default path and it succeeds (no root, no pre-created dir); (2) umount is idempotent and clears a dead mountpoint (proved by killing sshfs and re-running); (3) mounting an agent whose remote path does not exist REFUSES with a named cause and mounts nothing; (4) mounting an agent whose home is empty REFUSES (the empty-tree trap) rather than succeeding; (5) mount --json lists live mounts and a destroyed agent leaves none; (6) no mountpoint is left behind after any failure path; (7) battery VERIFY-PASS if any ssh/exec surface changed.

title: MOUNT NAMESPACE + WORKSPACE RESOLUTION: make the mount know WHICH project tree it is mounting, and validate it. There is no notion of a workspace, no way to mount a repo inside the agent's home rather than the whole home, and no check that the resolved workspace belongs to the namespace/project the session thinks it is working in. INTERPRETATION (say if this is wrong): 'namespace' = the fleet namespace/project owning the agent, 'workspace' = the tree inside it (the repo), and 'handle correctly' = resolve and validate both before mounting, and record them in the session binding so a session cannot mount one project's tree while believing it is another's. title: MOUNT DURABILITY: no phantom space, no silent disappearance, auto-recovery. Spec of record: docs/prd/SPEC-sshfs-mount-durability.md. MEASURED GAP TODAY (verified 2026-09-20 against internal/cli/mount.go): the mount passes ONLY StrictHostKeyChecking / UserKnownHostsFile / IdentitiesOnly - it passes NONE of the durability options sshfs supports (-o reconnect, -o auto_unmount, ServerAliveInterval/CountMax, ConnectTimeout, dir_cache), even though every OTHER ssh path in this repo (cp, ssh, deploy, session_probe, service) carries -o ConnectTimeout=10. Consequence: a transport blip is permanent, a dropped link leaves stale cached entries so a write appears to succeed into a kernel buffer and is lost (the PHANTOM SPACE), a crashed sshfs strands the mountpoint and blocks the next mount with 'not empty', and nothing detects any of it. The rule that keeps it safe: recovery may RE-ESTABLISH a mount, never RE-TARGET one, and running it twice leaves the same state as running it once; (5) CLEANUP THAT CANNOT BE FORGOTTEN: idempotent `bunker umount`, `bunker mount status`/--json listing every live mount as data (agent, mountpoint, remote path, namespace, pid, health, age), teardown hooks on agent destroy / session end / daemon shutdown, and an orphan sweep for mounts whose owning pid is gone (the mount-side twin of GAP-070's registry reconciliation); (6) state in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/bunker/mounts.json - per user, per boot, never a global registry. title: DYNAMIC PER-INSTANCE TARGETING (the 'new dynamic per bunker instance tools' half): make 'which bunker' a runtime value a session can discover, switch and hold, WITHOUT the tool list growing with the fleet. THE TENSION, RESOLVED EXPLICITLY: an earlier review said do not present 20 read tools for 20 bunkers; a later review asked for dynamic per-bunker-instance tools. Both are satisfied by keeping the CATALOG constant and making the INSTANCE SET dynamic: the tools stay fixed in shape with the target as an argument, while the set of instances a session may target is discovered at runtime and can change mid-session. What is dynamic is the instance REGISTRY and the session BINDING, never the tool catalog. DELIVERABLE: (1) instance discovery - enumerate the reachable bunker instances for this session (from the session profile's server list + the fleet inventory), with liveness and a one-line summary per instance, returned as DATA; (2) session binding - bind/unbind/switch the session's current target at runtime (explicit target wins per call; the binding is the default for that session only); (3) an instance-aware call path so ANY verb can be aimed at any bound instance without a new tool being registered - including a mount-backed mode and a verb-backed mode for the same instance, so both delivery paths reach the same tree; (4) refusal semantics - an unbound session refuses (GAP-093), an unknown instance refuses naming it, and a dead instance refuses as unreachable rather than silently retargeting; (5) no per-instance registration, no restart to pick up a new instance, and no global mutable current-server anywhere on the path. PASS: (1) with three instances known, a session switches between them mid-life and every verb follows the switch with zero cross-writes (proved against two real servers); (2) the offered tool list is byte-identical before and after an instance is added or removed (the constant-catalog proof, restated for instances); (3) the same tree is reachable in BOTH modes (mount-backed and verb-backed) and an edit made through one is visible through the other; (4) an unbound or unknown-instance call refuses with a distinct named cause and touches nothing; (5) two sessions bound to different instances run concurrently with zero interference; (6) discovery output is data (parseable), including explicitly 'unreachable' instances rather than omitting them.

title: [P1] SPEC: trust-tier preset model for agent sandboxing — tiers, config surface, precedence, and the experience-budget rule
reasoning: Design authority for the trust-tier preset family. Without a fixed tier model, precedence, and the experience-budget rule the implementation rows below improvise incompatible defaults.
detail:
Owner directive (Bane, 2026-09-20): bunker should ship a PRESET system for different levels of trust in the process/agent inside an agent host, with defaults chosen for a GOOD EXPERIENCE — explicitly neither the most locked-down nor the most open. This row is the DESIGN authority; GAP-117..122 implement it.

DELIVERABLE: docs/specs/safety-presets.md (implementation-ready).

(1) TIER MODEL — propose 4 tiers by trust, each a bundle across axes (resource bounds, memory-failure semantics, unit sandboxing, lifecycle atomicity, observability). Proposal (owner confirms the NAMES in review — naming is cheap, structure is not):
    open     — trusted operator's own agent on a dev box. STILL keeps a ceiling: a rogue fork/memory bomb must not take the host.
    standard — DEFAULT. The good-experience tier: an agent must still be able to run docker build, a compose stack, a .NET app, node/python workloads.
    guarded  — third-party / less-trusted agent code: standard + unit sandboxing + IO bounds.
    hostile  — adversarial tenant: guarded + strictest knobs. Control-plane features (exec recording, API lockdown) are GAP-074's `hardened.mode` and are NOT re-implemented here — this family owns the resource + unit-sandbox axis only. Boundary must be stated in the spec.

(2) KNOB MATRIX — which concrete knob each tier sets, per axis. The enforcement surface is BOTH (a) applyUserSliceLimits (internal/agent/manager_spawn.go:886-928: the always-on user-<uid>.slice drop-in that covers every `bunker exec` SSH session scope) and (b) buildRootlessArgs (internal/agent/isolation.go:109-139: the dockerd transient unit). The spec must state why one alone is insufficient — a unit-only limit lets exec sessions escape the ceiling; a slice-only limit leaves dockerd's argv inconsistent with its own ceiling.

(3) CONFIG SURFACE — global default in bunkerd config, per-spawn CLI override, env override, matching the existing containment.disclosure precedent (GAP-067): `safety.preset` global + `--preset` per-spawn + BUNKERD_SAFETY_PRESET. Precedence: per-spawn > global > built-in default. An unknown preset is a HARD ERROR, never a silent fallback.

(4) THE EXPERIENCE BUDGET RULE (core of the owner ask) — every knob a tier sets MUST carry a measured UX-cost line. A knob whose cost is unmeasured may NOT be default-on in any tier. The DEFAULT tier is chosen at the KNEE of the safety-vs-experience curve, with the measurement recorded in the spec — 'good experience' is a first-class acceptance criterion, not an afterthought.

(5) NO SILENT NO-OP — every applied knob must be verified write-then-read-back from the live cgroup/unit; if a preset's knob cannot be applied on this host, spawn FAILS LOUDLY (never half-armed). Rationale: the shadow-proc kernel-wave SEC review (2026-09-12, BLOCKER B2) measured a security property that attached successfully and then never fired — an unenforced default is worse than an absent one.

title: [P2] IMPL: atomic agent teardown via cgroup.kill — close the destroy race that leaves orphaned processes and held ports
reasoning: Destroy currently does systemctl stop + userdel -r and has a recurring documented race: orphaned docker-proxy holds mapped ports and userdel fails because a process is still alive, which then leaks the port allocation. cgroup.kill closes it atomically.
detail:
Replace the stop-then-userdel teardown with an atomic subtree kill as the first step.

BACKGROUND (documented, repeated incidents): 'Orphaned docker-proxy processes after container removal' hold mapped ports and block recreation with bind: address already in use; 'Destroy: systemctl targets wrong user instance' -> userdel fails because the process is still alive (the current workaround is a --force flag that skips the userdel error); 'A spawn that dies mid-step leaks a half-created USER'. The root cause is that stop-then-delete is not atomic against a forking process.

SCOPE: write 1 to cgroup.kill on the agent's cgroup (the user-<uid>.slice subtree) BEFORE the current stop/userdel sequence, then proceed as today. cgroup.kill atomically SIGKILLs the entire subtree — no forking process outruns it. Confirm availability on the fleet's systemd 259 / kernel 7.0 and fall back to the current path with a LOGGED warning only if unavailable (never silently).

PASS: (1) unit/integration test: a subtree containing a process that forks in a tight loop is fully reaped by the kill step; (2) the destroy path no longer needs --force to succeed in the orphan case (test with an orphaned docker-proxy held port); (3) a port held by an orphaned child is released after the atomic kill; (4) fallback path is exercised by a test and logs loudly; (5) go test ./... green + bundle VERIFY-PASS.
review_notes: PASS: (1) fork-loop subtree fully reaped by the kill step; (2) destroy succeeds without --force in the orphan case; (3) port released after atomic kill; (4) fallback path tested and logs loudly; (5) go test ./... green + bundle VERIFY-PASS. Fix direction: kill-then-delete; never silently skip the kill.

  (b) A minimal program mirroring runWithTimeout exactly:

title: [P1] spawned agents can NEVER use the shared scratch exchange: the root is created 0750 root:root (not 2750 root:bunker-agents) and nothing but `host-provision --apply` ever fixes it
reasoning:
README §Agent isolation and specs/agent-tmp-isolation.md document the cross-agent exchange point as the
only sanctioned hand-off between agents:
  bunker exec a -- sh -c 'cp build.tar /srv/bunker-share/a/build.tar'
  bunker exec b -- cp /srv/bunker-share/a/build.tar ./build.tar
On a host where the exchange root was never bootstrapped by `bunker host-provision --apply`, the daemon's
spawn path (internal/agent/isolation.go:209 -> hostsetup.EnsureAgentScratch) creates each agent's capped
tmpfs directory UNDER a root that the agent cannot traverse. No error is raised, the daemon logs
'shared scratch ready', and every documented exchange command fails with EACCES.
detail:
MEASURED LIVE 2026-09-20 on bunker-las-03 (daemon 0.1.4 commit 6a6ad20, reports isolation-grant; HEAD CLI 93d7a53).

Host view (root):
  /srv/bunker-share                 root:root    mode 750   <-- created 2026-09-20 03:26 by an operator/manual step
  /srv/bunker-share/df1017a         bunker-df1017a:bunker-agents  drwxrws---  tmpfs size=262144k
  /srv/bunker-share/df1017b         bunker-df1017b:bunker-agents  drwxrws---  tmpfs size=262144k
  the per-agent dirs at 2770 ARE the documented shape; the root is NOT (docs: 'root-owned, setgid to the
  agent group and NOT writable by it, mode 2750').

Agent view (three separate agents):
  id -> uid=1001(bunker-df1017a) gid=1001 groups=...,989(bunker-agents)   (membership is correct)
  ls -la /srv/bunker-share        -> Permission denied
  ls -la /srv/bunker-share/df1017a -> Permission denied
  echo X > /srv/bunker-share/df1017a/probe.txt -> Permission denied
  cp /etc/hostname /srv/bunker-share/df1017c/build.tar -> Permission denied
So a spawn reports 'shared scratch ready', the cap is mounted, and the feature is 100% unusable.

WHY: EnsureAgentScratch assumes the root exists with the right mode; only Options.EnsureSharedScratch
(hostsetup/scratch.go:81, which chowns root:<group>, chmods 2750 and STATS the result back as a hard error)
creates it correctly - and its only caller is internal/hostsetup/status.go:219, i.e. `bunker host-provision
--apply`. The per-agent path (which runs on every spawn) never calls it. The comment on
EnsureAgentScratch claims it provisions the root, but the code does MkdirAll on the AGENT dir only.

CONTROL: the same documented layout EXISTS and works on bunker-mvp:
  /srv/bunker-share  mode=2750 owner=root:bunker-agents
and is absent entirely on bunker-las-01 (mode 750 root:root), bunker-las-02 and bunker-las-04 (no
/srv/bunker-share at all) - so this is a host-provisioning gap that hits most of the fleet, not a one-off.

IMPACT: the bounded exchange point is the mechanism for multi-agent hand-off, and it silently never works
unless somebody remembered to run host-provision --apply on that host. Failure mode is 'Permission denied'
from the agent side with a green 'shared scratch ready' on the daemon side.

FIX DIRECTION (one of): (a) make the per-agent path call EnsureSharedScratch (or at least verify the root's
mode and fail the scratch step loudly, since a scratch the agent cannot reach is not 'ready'); (b) fail the
spawn with an actionable error naming `bunker host-provision --apply`; or (c) treat a root not at 2750 as a

title: [P2] `bunker env set/get` rejects `--server` in every position except before the subcommand, and the success path exits 0 having set nothing
reasoning:
`bunker env set <agent-id> KEY=VALUE` counts positional args AFTER the flag parse, so a trailing or
interleaved --server is consumed as the KEY=VALUE argument and the command refuses with
'env set requires exactly one KEY=VALUE argument'. Only `bunker env --server X set <id> K=V` works -
the one position the README never shows.
detail:
MEASURED LIVE 2026-09-20 (HEAD 93d7a53, bunker-las-03):
  bunker env --server bunker-las-03 set df1017a K1=v1   -> rc=0   (works, nothing printed)
  bunker env set df1017a K2=v2 --server bunker-las-03   -> 'env set requires exactly one KEY=VALUE argument' rc=1
  bunker env set --server bunker-las-03 df1017a K3=v3   -> same refusal                                rc=1
  bunker env get df1017a K2 --server bunker-las-03      -> 'env get requires exactly one KEY argument'    rc=1
  bunker exec --server bunker-las-03 df1017a -- sh -c 'echo "K1=$K1 K2=$K2 K3=$K3"' -> K1=v1 K2= K3=

So the documented `bunker env set abc12345 KEY=VALUE` (README §Use the CLI) only works when the server is
already the active one or the flag is placed FIRST - and the failure message does not mention that the
--server value was parsed as an argument, which is what the user needs to know.

receive, so a swallowed --server is visible.

title: [P0 SECURITY] sshfs 3.7.3 on BOTH ends is in the CVE-2026-47187 (CVSS 9.3) / CVE-2026-48711 affected range - a rogue or compromised agent can read/write the CLIENT's local files through the mount

title: [P1] Decide the mount protocol on evidence: benchmark sshfs vs the real alternatives for OUR shape (NFSv4 over an SSH tunnel, rclone mount SFTP, Taildrive if Tailscale is in use, virtiofs if the agent becomes a microVM)
source: research 2026-09-20 (mount protocol review, Bane question: 'was SSHFS right?')
reasoning: sshfs was the right STARTING choice and it still is the right DEFAULT: zero server-side daemon, it reuses the SSH key/identity we already provision per agent, it inherits SSH's auth and the agent's uid confinement, and it needs nothing installed on the agent beyond sftp-server. Every alternative buys performance or multi-writer semantics by giving up one of those. So the decision is not 'replace sshfs' but 'know the threshold at which each alternative wins, and make the mount pluggable so we can switch per workload'.
detail: Candidate matrix to measure (all against a real agent, same workload as MOUNT-003): (1) sshfs - baseline; (2) NFSv4 exported from the agent and tunneled over SSH (kernel client, real POSIX, caching, but needs a server + privileged port + export config in the agent, which widens the agent's surface); (3) rclone mount with the SFTP backend - keeps the SSH model, adds VFS caching and SFTP pipelining, upstream-measured much faster on high latency (sshfs issue #300); (4) Taildrive (Tailscale WebDAV) - node-to-node file sharing with ACLs, only relevant IF the agents are tailnet nodes, which today they are not; (5) virtiofs - the right answer the moment an agent is a microVM rather than a userland process, and the benchmark leader there (9p is the one to avoid). Deliverable: a one-page decision record with a measured number per row and a named threshold, plus the pluggability seam in the CLI so the choice is data, not a rewrite.

title: [P2] Watch-list of hot upcoming filesystem options worth playing with: FUSE passthrough, FUSE io_uring zero-copy series, SMB over QUIC (kernel cifs/ksmbd), and JuiceFS/SeaweedFS for persistent multi-bunker workspaces
reasoning: Bane asked what is new/hot to play with. Ranked by how soon it could matter to us: kernel/transport improvements (adopt for free as hosts upgrade), then protocol shifts (decision points), then distributed-FS products (relevant only if we want workspaces that outlive one agent and are shared by many).
detail: 1. FUSE passthrough (Linux 6.9+, CONFIG_FUSE_PASSTHROUGH=y - PRESENT on the control host) bypasses the FUSE daemon per-file: big win for stacked LOCAL filesystems, NOT available for a network FS like sshfs, so it is relevant to agent-internal mounts rather than the agent mount itself. 2. FUSE io_uring buffer/zero-copy patch series (linux-fsdevel, Apr 2026) + vfs_fadvise forwarding (Sep 2026) - still landing, watch, and pick up via libfuse/kernel upgrades. 3. SMB over QUIC: Samba shipped full support and the kernel cifs/ksmbd series landed (2026-04); it is a UDP/443 transport with kernel-TLS handshaking - interesting mainly for crossing hostile networks without a VPN, which we do not need internally (we have Tailscale/WireGuard). 4. JuiceFS / SeaweedFS expose POSIX (FUSE + kernel mount, hardlinks, atomic rename) over distributed storage and are explicitly being marketed at agent workspaces in 2026: this is the answer if/when 'deploy any number of bunkers' means agents SHARING one workspace tree with consistent rename/lock semantics - sshfs cannot do multi-writer at all. Do not build any of this now; this row exists so the option is on the record with its trigger condition rather than rediscovered later.

title: [P1] DECISION RECORD: the toolsd integration point is DELIVERY (toolsd binary in the agent over the exec path) - NOT a linked library, NOT an HTTP daemon in the agent
source: Bane design question 2026-09-20 (integration point is up to us, made correct)
reasoning: The three shapes were: (a) add an HTTP server to toolsd and have bunkerd proxy to it; (b) treat toolsd as a Go library and call it in-process from bunkerd; (c) deliver the toolsd binary to the agent and invoke it via exec. (b) puts the file WRITE in the wrong privilege domain: bunkerd runs as root on the host while the agent's tree belongs to an unprivileged uid, so every edit would land as root, bypassing the uid confinement, private /tmp (GAP-075), cgroup and network policy this project exists to provide - the shape of a privilege-escalation bug. (b) also cannot reach a second host, and it version-locks two independently deployed repos. (a) buys nothing the exec path does not already give: it adds a listening service inside the untrusted domain, a second credential and lifecycle, and a side channel invisible to the audit chain.
detail: Decision record: docs/prd/ADR-toolsd-integration.md. Chosen: (c), consumed as a CLI + JSON-descriptor contract (toolsd describe --json), with the binary delivered agent-side by GAP-096 and structured payloads riding stdin (bunker exec --stdin, enabled by GAP-094), never quoted argv. bunker gains NO compile-time dependency on coding-hermes-tools. MEASURED EVIDENCE for the library rejection: every toolsd package is under internal/, and a throwaway module with a replace directive fails to build with 'use of internal package .../internal/fsops not allowed' (control build in the same module passed). Adopting the library requires refactoring coding-hermes-tools to widen its public API first. Also recorded: the verb path deliberately shares ONE filesystem view of truth with the sshfs mount (both operate in the agent), so the two reading paths cannot diverge on concurrent edits. Stated limitation: fsops confinement is cooperative inside toolsd; the hard boundary remains the agent's uid + cgroup + namespace.

title: [P1] MOUNT DRIVER SEAM (prerequisite for rclone + io_uring): the mount command is a hardcoded server-side sshfs string, so there is no driver abstraction to add a driver to
reasoning: Measured: NO driver abstraction exists anywhere (grep for mountdriver/driver/MountType returns nothing). Everything downstream of that string is sshfs-specific: the retry constants, the permanent-vs-transient output classifier, and the reconnect handling. Adding a driver without a seam means bolt-on string sniffing on the client.
detail: Deliver a driver seam, keeping sshfs the DEFAULT and old clients working. (1) proto: carry an explicit driver identity alongside (not instead of) the existing command string, so an older client still reads the sshfs default and a newer one dispatches on the driver; prefer a structured mount spec over a second opaque string. (2) server: emit the command for the selected driver; the selection must be requestable on spawn/mount and default to sshfs. (3) client: dispatch per driver instead of assuming sshfs. (4) THE TRAP TO CLOSE EXPLICITLY: the durability layer (bounded attempts, sshfsPermanentFragments / sshfsTransientFragments classification, mount.go) is sshfs-SHAPED. A new driver that silently inherits it gets nonsense classification, and a new driver that skips it silently loses GAP-107's guarantees. Each driver must declare its own classifier (or explicitly declare 'none, with reason'), and that must be asserted by a test. (5) The binding verify reports the active driver + its version + its capabilities, so a client/driver mismatch is a named warning, not a silent behaviour split. Cross-ref MOUNT-007, MOUNT-008, GAP-107.

title: [P1] OPT-IN DRIVER: rclone mount with the SFTP backend — no server-side change, and it brings the VFS cache + pipelining options sshfs lacks
reasoning: Bane's constraint is that a new driver must not require a new server. rclone satisfies it exactly: it speaks SFTP to the sshd/sftp-server the agent already runs, so the agent gets NOTHING installed — only the client needs the rclone binary. The payoff is the option set: VFS caching, directory cache, read-ahead chunking, write-back, transfer/checker concurrency and SFTP-specific toggles, i.e. the knobs that make a remote tree usable as an editing surface rather than a latency- bound one. Upstream issue libfuse/sshfs#300 measures sshfs as far slower than rclone over high-latency links because sshfs cannot pipeline SFTP.
detail: Implement rclone as a selectable, NON-DEFAULT driver on the MOUNT-006 seam. Requirements: (1) NO CONFIG FILE — use an inline backend spec so there is no rclone.conf and no credential file to manage: `rclone mount :sftp,host=<host>,user=<agent-user>,key_file=<per-agent-key>,shell_type=unix:/ <mountpoint>`; pass the flag set with `--` (`:sftp` starts with a colon, so a bare invocation can be parsed as a flag). (2) Expose the extra options (documented, not hidden): --vfs-cache-mode off|minimal|writes|full, --dir-cache-time, --vfs-cache-max-size, --vfs-cache-max-age, --vfs-write-back, --vfs-read-chunk-size[-limit], --buffer-size, --transfers, --checkers, --umask, --sftp-set-modtime, --sftp-disable-hashcheck. (3) Version pin: the distro candidate here is 1.60.1 (old) — pin explicitly and prefer the current official static binary; record the pinned version in the binding verify. (4) RECONCILE, do not stack, the retry logic: rclone has its own --retries/--low-level-retries while the CLI has an sshfs-shaped bounded-retry classifier; pick ONE owner per failure class and say so. (5) Prove the no-new-server claim by measuring the agent before and after (installed packages, listening sockets, credentials) — it must be byte-identical. (6) Benchmark against sshfs on the SAME workload as MOUNT-003 (find, git status, N-file read/write) and record the numbers. (7) Document in docs/mount-drivers.md + README mount section.
review_notes: PASS: `bunker mount` with the rclone driver succeeds against a real agent with NO change to that agent's installed packages, listening sockets or credentials (proved by a before/after diff); at least --vfs-cache-mode and --dir-cache-time are reachable and documented; the pinned rclone version is reported; a raw before/after benchmark against sshfs is recorded; and a failure classifier is assigned per rule (4) of MOUNT-006.

title: [P1] OPT-IN DRIVER: FUSE over io_uring — kernel-side ready on the control host, but our packaged libfuse does NOT expose the transport, so this is verify-then-enable
reasoning: FUSE over io_uring moves the kernel<->userspace channel onto io_uring and cuts per-request overhead (measured ~1.4-2.8x on suitable workloads). It costs nothing server-side — it is a property of the host that MOUNTS — so it satisfies Bane's constraint. But it needs THREE things together and we currently have one: the kernel (yes, locally), a libfuse BUILT with the io_uring transport (NO — measured), and the module parameter enabled (not yet set). Measured: no `io_uring`/`iouring` string in libfuse3.so.3, fusermount3, mount.fuse3 or sshfs on the control host (libfuse 3.18.2), while the control kernel 7.0.0-30 has CONFIG_FUSE_IO_URING=y and the daemon host runs 6.8.0-117 with no io_uring FUSE. So the deliverable is a capability probe plus an opt-in, NOT an assumption.
detail: Implement as an opt-in mount option on the MOUNT-006 seam, non-default. (1) CAPABILITY PROBE: detect kernel CONFIG_FUSE_IO_URING (or /sys/module/fuse/parameters/enableuring presence) AND that the libfuse/sshfs build actually accepts the transport; when either is missing, REFUSE with a named reason naming which of the three prerequisites is absent — never silently mount without it. (2) ENABLEMENT: `echo 1 > /sys/module/fuse/parameters/enableuring` then mount with `-o iouring`; document that the sysfs write needs privilege (and how to make it persistent, or why not to). (3) If the packaged libfuse cannot do it, provide the build path (libfuse built with io_uring support) as an explicit, documented option rather than a silent no-op — same shape as MOUNT-009's patched-sshfs option. (4) MEASURE: before/after on the MOUNT-003 workload, recorded as numbers. (5) Record per-host availability honestly: control host kernel-ready/build-not-ready, daemon host not-ready (6.8). (6) Document in docs/mount-drivers.md §3.3. Extends/absorbs MOUNT-003 (whose research this implements).
review_notes: PASS: on a host lacking any prerequisite the option REFUSES naming which prerequisite is missing (three distinct messages); on a host where all three hold, the mount succeeds with the io_uring transport active (proved by the mount option in the command and a recorded kernel/config/libfuse triple); a before/after benchmark is recorded; and the per-host availability table in docs/mount-drivers.md matches the live hosts.

title: [P1] TOPOLOGY: one daemon per USER (recommended), not per SESSION -- N per-session daemons over one tree reintroduce the lost-update class the lease registry exists to prevent
source: Bane 2026-09-20 (toolsd surfaces proposal) -- the load-bearing decision it glosses
reasoning: 'Multiple sockets for multiple connections' is true of the TRANSPORT and dangerous as a STATE MODEL: N concurrent sessions would mean N daemons with N independent in-memory states over ONE tree. That is exactly the failure internal/lease was built for -- the cross-session registry is a shared FILE precisely because no shared process exists today. Multiple daemons each believing they own state would silently undo that protection.
detail: Decide and implement ONE of: (a) ONE daemon per USER, socket-activated, with later sessions connecting to the same socket -- shared state may then live in memory safely, and leases finally get what they have been faking: liveness tied to a real connection (CHT-030's 'the CLI's default pid is the TRANSIENT parent' is a symptom of having no daemon). RECOMMENDED. Or (b) per-session daemons with ALL shared state remaining in FILES as today, so the daemon holds no state authority and buys only the spawn saving and streaming. Either way the invariant is unchanged and must be re-proved through the NEW path: two concurrent sessions produce exactly ONE lease grant and one refusal naming the holder (CHT-007; remote CHT-052).

title: [P2] ONE IDL with GENERATED surfaces (Connect RPC primary; REST/JSON + OpenAPI derived) -- NOT six hand-written protocol servers, and no QUIC
source: Bane 2026-09-20 (toolsd surfaces proposal): 'a few surfaces ... openapi surfaces that we maintain'
reasoning: Six surfaces carrying the same verbs multiplies auth paths, error mappings and the test matrix for almost no functional gain. Per protocol: QUIC is the clearest no -- its entire value is surviving lossy or path-changing NETWORKS, while here the transport is a unix socket over an already-reliable, already-encrypted SSH channel, so it adds a handshake, TLS config and real complexity for zero benefit. WebSocket earns its place only with server-to-client PUSH, and even then SSE over the same HTTP/2 socket is one code path instead of two. HTTP/2 vs HTTP/1.1 is pick-one, not both. gRPC/Connect is the strong candidate because bunker ALREADY uses connectrpc for its daemon<->CLI protocol, so reusing that IDL toolchain is the lowest marginal cost and it generates typed clients. REST/JSON is the strong candidate for debuggability: curl --unix-socket is the single best property a remote surface can have.
detail: Implement the surface as ONE protobuf IDL plus Connect RPC over the socket. Derive any REST/JSON bridge and the OpenAPI document FROM THAT IDL with a generator, and add a CI drift check that fails the build when the generated artefacts are stale -- the discipline bunker already applies to its proto, and that toolsd applies to docs/reference.md via cmd/gendocs (both prove the pattern works here). Store the spec of record in DuckBrain. Explicit non-goals: no QUIC; no WebSocket unless a push need is demonstrated; no second hand-written server.

title: [P1] TOPOLOGY: one daemon per USER (recommended), not per SESSION -- N sessions -> N daemons -> N independent in-memory states over one tree is what internal/lease exists to prevent. Re-prove: two sessions -> exactly one grant, one refusal naming the holder.

The proven mechanism sidesteps it: one SOCKET per user at %t/toolsd.sock, and with Accept=yes each CONNECTION gets its own short-lived process -- so there is no long-lived per-session daemon holding state at all, and nothing is shared in memory between connections. The 'one daemon per user' recommendation is therefore moot for the MCP surface: the state that must not fork (the lease registry) has to live in FILES regardless, because even a per-user daemon would have to survive a connection ending. WHAT REMAINS: prove the invariant that actually matters -- two concurrent connections over this socket yield exactly ONE lease grant and one refusal NAMING the holder -- and confirm the lease registry's cross-process story (CHT-030's finding that 'the CLI's default pid is the TRANSIENT parent' is a symptom worth re-checking when the caller is socket-activated rather than a shell).
detail: Measured: per-connection activation confirmed (0 processes before connect). Because each connection is a separate process, a lease held by connection A must be visible to connection B, or the whole point of internal/lease is lost -- that is the test this row now owes. Do NOT assume the file-backed registry is already correct across processes; prove it with two live concurrent connections.
review_notes: PASS: two concurrent connections to one agent's socket produce exactly one lease grant and one refusal naming the holder, demonstrated with the socket-activated processes (not with two shells on the client).

title: [P1] AUDIT CONTINUITY -- solve BEFORE the first verb ships: a private socket bypasses the daemon, so remote edits can vanish from the hash-chained audit trail (GAP-047..050, attribution GAP-095). Gate, not an afterthought.

Whichever is chosen, the audit trail must record the SAME facts it records today: who, what verb, what path, and under what confinement root.

title: [P1] END TO END: the remote file tools working on an agent over the proven socket recipe -- one command makes an agent socket-ready, and read/write/edit/edit-advanced work through it. THE HOW IS ALREADY SOLVED AND WRITTEN DOWN; this row is 'execute the recipe', not 'design the recipe'.

What is NOT yet true is that an operator can get there without hand-writing files. The row's job is to make the recipe a SUPPORTED, REPEATABLE path and to prove the end state. Measured baseline to reach: socket active at %t/toolsd.sock owned by the agent at 0600, ZERO toolsd processes before the first connect (connection-activated), initialize -> {"name":"toolsd","version":...}, tools/list -> 20 tools including toolsd_read/toolsd_write/toolsd_list plus toolsd_patch/toolsd_apply/toolsd_diff3/toolsd_lease, and a real toolsd_write + toolsd_read round-trip succeeding over the socket. No TCP listener, nothing as root, no long-lived daemon holding state (Accept=yes = one short-lived process PER CONNECTION). The daemon is NOT in the data path; its role is a file drop. PRECONDITIONS FROM THE RECIPE THAT WILL BITE: run systemctl --user via `bunker exec`, never from the host (the host cannot address the agent's user manager by name); use %t and %h, never a hardcoded /run/user path; the artifact must be static (make dist refuses otherwise) or it dies on the far side; the agent's $HOME is the destination because the server already puts $HOME/bin on every exec PATH. BLOCKERS THAT ARE NOT THIS ROW'S TO SOLVE: audit continuity (SURF-004) gates any MUTATING verb, and the lease invariant across two concurrent connections (SURF-003) is unproven -- this row may ship read verbs first.
